paras: The Mulberry railroad workers shooting incident was an episode in late August 1903 in which residents of Mulberry fired pistols to drive Black railroad construction workers out of the town and back to their cars. No one was reported killed or injured, and the local Van Buren Press, the only paper found to report it, said that rumors of a "wholesale slaughter of negroes" had been made "nearly out of whole cloth."

In the summer of 1903 contractors for the Missouri Pacific railroad were employing what the Van Buren Press called "a great many negroes" in reconstruction work along the line. According to the same paper, Mulberry claimed to be "a white town—i. e. one that wants no negroes."

On a Saturday, about August 22, the workers' construction cars were set out at Mulberry, and the Black laborers, in the paper's words, "overran the town." This "did not suit some of the citizens," who fired their pistols "for the purpose of running the Africans back to their cars." The account does not say how many people fired or whether anyone was hit.

On Monday morning, reports of "race troubles at Mulberry the previous night" were hawked about Van Buren and grew into a story of mass killing, which the Press dismissed as nearly fabricated. A week later Charley Wells, visiting Van Buren, said the reports had been "greatly exaggerated," that there was "very little to them," and that the participants were "a crowd of boys." No report of arrests or any official response appears in the coverage.

The episode is known only from two local briefs in the Van Buren Press, printed among social notes and town news on August 29 and September 5, 1903. The paper's concern was the rumor rather than the shooting: it stated Mulberry's exclusion of Black residents without comment, described the workers as having "overran the town," and called them "Africans." Its second notice further minimized the affair by attributing it to boys.
No wire report or Black-press account of the episode was found.
The two notices differ over who took part: the first attributed the shooting to "some of the citizens" of Mulberry, while Wells described the participants as "a crowd of boys."

bases: Townspeople fired pistols to drive Black railroad construction workers out of Mulberry back to their cars; no one is reported killed or hurt (A1, A2).

Both reports come from one local weekly, the Van Buren Press; the first describes the shooting (A1) and the second, from an informant, only says the reports were exaggerated and the participants were boys (A2).

accounts.label: Rumor in Van Buren
accounts.gist: Reports hawked about Van Buren on Monday morning spoke of race troubles at Mulberry, enlarged into 'a wholesale slaughter of negroes'.

accounts.label: Van Buren Press account
accounts.gist: Black construction workers came into a town that 'wants no negroes', and some citizens fired pistols to run them back to their cars; the slaughter story was 'nearly out of whole cloth'.

accounts.label: Charley Wells
accounts.gist: The reports were greatly exaggerated, there was very little to them, and the participants were a crowd of boys.

framing.detail: The Van Buren Press debunked the slaughter rumor but described the workers as having 'overran the town', called them 'Africans', and stated Mulberry's exclusion of Black residents without comment; a week later it minimized the affair as the work of 'a crowd of boys'.

versions.value: Some of the citizens of Mulberry fired pistols
The participants were a crowd of boys and there was very little to the reports

conflicts.note: Both versions appear in the same paper; the second is secondhand from one visitor and does not describe what happened.

versions.value: Pistols fired to drive workers back; no casualties mentioned

conflicts.note: The paper reported the rumor only to deny it; no other source on casualties was found.

record_check.dossier: About 1903-08-22 to 1903-08-23: cars set out Saturday, trouble reported Monday morning as of 'the previous night'
The papers do not name the county or state of Mulberry; the only source is the Van Buren (Ark.) weekly treating it as a nearby town
Unnamed Black construction laborers employed by Missouri Pacific contractors; victim_race should be Black
'Some of the citizens' of Mulberry (A1), or 'a crowd of boys' (A2); no size given
'Overran the town' is the paper's own characterization of Black workers entering a town that 'wants no negroes'; it should be quoted, not stated as fact
2 issues of the Van Buren Press (1903-08-29 and 1903-09-05)
Railroad reconstruction labor force entering a town that excluded Black residents

info: Construction cars were set out at Mulberry on a Saturday (about 1903-08-22); reports reaching Van Buren on Monday morning (about 1903-08-24) placed the trouble on 'the previous night' (about 1903-08-23).
Mulberry (state and county not named in the text; reported in the Van Buren, Arkansas, weekly as a nearby town)
Unnamed Black laborers employed by Missouri Pacific contractors on reconstruction work, who had arrived on construction cars
'Some of the citizens' of Mulberry (A1); 'a crowd of boys' according to Charley Wells (A2)
None reported; a rumored 'wholesale slaughter of negroes' was described as nearly fabricated
